query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of Blue

Blue is everywhere now: jeans, passports, corporate logos, police uniforms, hospital signs, social media icons, and the sky above them all. But for much of human history, blue was strangely elusive. It surrounded people in nature, yet it was difficult to capture, name, and use.

In many ancient cultures, blue was not a common pigment. The sky and sea were visible, of course, but making a stable blue dye or paint was hard. Earth gives up reds, browns, yellows, and blacks more readily than blue. Ochre, charcoal, and clay could be used by early humans, but blue required rarer materials or complex processes.

One of the earliest prized blues came from **lapis lazuli**, a deep blue stone mined in what is now Afghanistan. Ancient traders carried it across long distances to Mesopotamia, Egypt, and later Europe. In Egypt, blue became associated with divinity, protection, and the heavens. Egyptians also developed **Egyptian blue**, one of the first synthetic pigments, made by heating silica, copper, calcium, and alkali. It appeared in tomb paintings, statues, jewelry, and sacred objects.

In the ancient Mediterranean world, blue had mixed status. The Greeks and Romans used blue pigments, but they did not always prize the colour as later Europeans would. In Rome, blue could be associated with foreigners, barbarians, or lower status clothing. Reds, purples, whites, and golds often carried greater prestige.

During the Middle Ages, blue rose dramatically in importance. This change was partly religious. The Virgin Mary began to be painted wearing rich blue robes, especially in Western Christian art. The pigment used for the finest works was **ultramarine**, made from ground lapis lazuli. Its name meant “from beyond the sea,” because it came to Europe through distant trade routes. Ultramarine was so expensive that patrons sometimes specified its use in contracts. To paint Mary in blue was not just an artistic choice; it was a declaration of reverence, wealth, and devotion.

Blue also became a royal and aristocratic colour. In France, it was linked to the monarchy, especially through heraldry. Over time, blue acquired meanings of loyalty, truth, and dignity. This was a major shift: a colour once relatively marginal became one of the most honoured in European visual culture.

The history of blue is also the history of dyes. In Europe, **woad** was used to dye cloth blue. Later, indigo from Asia and the Americas became a major global commodity. Indigo produced a stronger, deeper blue than woad and became central to trade, colonial economies, and enslaved labor. Like sugar, cotton, and tobacco, blue dye was bound up with empire and exploitation.

In the modern era, blue became more democratic. The invention of synthetic dyes in the nineteenth century transformed colour production. Blue was no longer dependent on rare stones or labor-intensive plants. It could be manufactured, standardized, and sold widely. This changed fashion, printing, painting, industry, and everyday life.

Artists also remade blue. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, new pigments expanded the palette: cobalt blue, Prussian blue, cerulean, and synthetic ultramarine. Blue became the colour of atmosphere, melancholy, spirituality, and abstraction. Picasso’s Blue Period used it to evoke poverty and sorrow. Yves Klein later created International Klein Blue, a vivid ultramarine associated with immateriality and pure sensation.

Blue entered politics and identity as well. It appears in many national flags, often representing liberty, vigilance, justice, or the sea and sky. In the United States, blue is linked to the Union, the Democratic Party, police uniforms, and “blue-collar” labor. In Britain and parts of Europe, it has often been associated with conservatism. Its meanings shift depending on place and context.

Today, blue is often described as the world’s favourite colour. It suggests calm, trust, intelligence, cleanliness, distance, and stability. That is why banks, technology companies, airlines, and health organizations use it so frequently. Yet blue also carries sadness: “feeling blue,” the blues, blue notes, blue moods.

The history of blue is therefore a story of transformation. It began as a difficult colour to obtain, rare in pigment and dye. It became sacred, royal, commercial, industrial, emotional, and global. Blue moved from stone and sky into cloth, canvas, screen, and symbol. It is now ordinary enough to wear every day, yet still powerful enough to suggest infinity.
